gap: No result ChatGPT got states that on 2026-11-27 a 45 W-class charger sold for the same $15.99 as the 30 W Anker Nano it picked (Anker Nano Charger Neo, 'Dynamic 45W - 65W', on Amazon), while Anker's own spec table caps the Nano 30W's PPS at 16 V.
standout_why: Compared against TechGearLab's Anker Nano 30W review (cited), Android Authority's best-chargers page (cited) and Anker's A2147 page (in the results). TechGearLab prints a $16 list price and says the Nano 30W is 'not the best charger for the iPhone 18 Pro and above' but names no under-$20 charger that is faster. Android Authority prints $22.99 for the Nano 3 and says it cannot give the 20 V a Pixel 9 Pro XL needs; its 45 W options are $27.42 and $29.99. Neither page prices a 45 W charger under $20. Tom's Hardware's page (cited) could not be read: the fetch returned only navigation. Standout is held at 2 because the Neo's AVS support rests on Notebookcheck's news report of Anker's claim, with no spec sheet or ChargerLAB test and no named reviewer's measurement.
decides: It challenges ChatGPT's pick but does not overturn it on sourced evidence. At the same $15.99, the Neo offers 45 W or more against the Nano's 30 W, so the Nano 30W loses on watts to one device, the first figure buyers decide on. The Nano 30W keeps the tested-pick position (TechGearLab measured 29.4 W; Android Authority measured 27 W over PPS) until a named test or spec sheet confirms the Neo's output. Belkin's 30W loses because its own page lists no PPS. For our row: the linked UGREEN Nexode Air 65W is $24.99, over the line. The partner-store Nexode Air 45W ($15.19 per the cluster map) is the only candidate of ours, and I could not open its page today (HTTP 429 and 403), so its price and specs must be reread before it is featured. If it cannot be confirmed under $20, the page is a skip.
